title: For Loops
overview: Repetition is one of the most powerful things a computer can do. A task that would take you hours — done in milliseconds. For loops let you repeat an action over a sequence of items, making your programs dramatically more powerful.

blocks.content: Imagine you need to wish all 50 students in your class a happy birthday. Without loops, you'd write 50 separate print statements. With a loop, you write one.
A **for loop** repeats a block of code for each item in a sequence. The loop goes through the items one by one, running the same instructions each time.

The syntax:
```
for variable in sequence:
    do this
```
Each time the loop runs, `variable` holds the current item from the sequence.

blocks.title: Try It — Your First Loop
blocks.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]

for fruit in fruits:
    print(fruit)

print("Loop complete!")

blocks.content: The loop ran 3 times — once for each item. Each time, `fruit` held a different item: first `"apple"`, then `"banana"`, then `"cherry"`.
The code after the loop (`print("Loop complete!")`) runs once, after all iterations are done.

analogy.title: Attendance Roll Call
analogy.description: A teacher calls out student names one by one from the register. For each name, they perform the same action: mark present or absent. A for loop does exactly this — iterate through a list, performing the same action on each item.
bullets: The teacher reads each name from the list, one by one.
For every name, the same action is taken — present or absent.
The process repeats until every student has been checked.
analogy.highlightCard: A for loop goes through each item in a list and runs the same code for each one.

visualization.title: For Loop Iteration
bullets: for item in list: visits each element of the list in order.
The variable 'item' holds the current element on each pass.
Python repeats the loop body once for every element in the list.
visualization.highlightCard: for item in collection: — the simplest and most powerful loop in Python.

The indented block runs once for every item in the students list.

code.highlightCard: for loops eliminate repetition — write the logic once, Python applies it to every item.

reflection.question: How many times does a for loop run if the sequence has 5 items?

blocks.content: What if you don't have a list, but you just want to repeat something a specific number of times?
Python's `range()` function generates a sequence of numbers on demand. It's the most common way to control how many times a loop runs.

`range(5)` generates: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (starts at 0, stops before 5)

`range(1, 6)` generates: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (start, stop — stops before stop)

`range(0, 10, 2)` generates: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 (start, stop, step)

blocks.title: Try It — range() Variations
blocks.code:
# Count from 1 to 5
for i in range(1, 6):
    print(i)

print("---")

# Even numbers from 0 to 10
for num in range(0, 11, 2):
    print(num)

blocks.title: Try It — Countdown

# Countdown from 5 to 1
for i in range(5, 0, -1):
    print(i)
print("Blast off!")

analogy.title: Alarm Clock Snooze Button
analogy.description: You set your alarm to ring 5 times, starting at 6:00 AM, every 10 minutes. range(6, 11, 1) works like this: start time, end time, interval. You know exactly how many times it will repeat.
bullets: The alarm goes off for the first time and you hit snooze.
It rings again after 9 minutes — you hit snooze again.
This repeats a fixed number of times before you finally get up.
analogy.highlightCard: range() creates a sequence of numbers your for loop can count through.

visualization.title: range(1, 6)
bullets: range(5) generates 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — five numbers starting from 0.
range(1, 6) generates 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 — start included, stop excluded.
range(start, stop, step) lets you count by any interval you choose.
visualization.highlightCard: range(1, 6) counts from 1 to 5 — the stop value is never included.

highlights: range(1, 6) creates numbers 1 through 5 — the 6 is excluded.
i takes each value from range in order: 1, then 2, then 3, and so on.
range() is memory-efficient — it generates numbers one at a time, not all at once.
code.highlightCard: range() gives your for loop a precise count — start, stop, and step.

reflection.question: What does range(2, 10, 3) generate?
reflection.answer: 2, 5, 8 — starts at 2, adds 3 each time, stops before 10.

blocks.content: Once you have the basics down, a few patterns show up in almost every Python program.
**Accumulation:** Start with a value and build it up inside a loop. This is how you calculate sums, products, and totals.

blocks.title: Try It — Summing Numbers
blocks.code:
marks = [78, 85, 92, 67, 88]
total = 0

for mark in marks:
    total = total + mark

average = total / len(marks)
print(f"Total: {total}")
print(f"Average: {average}")

blocks.content: **Enumerate:** When you need both the index and the value, use `enumerate()`. It gives you both at once.

analogy.title: Bank Passbook
analogy.description: Your passbook accumulates transactions: each deposit adds to the running total. A for loop with an accumulator variable works the same — each iteration adds to or builds on the previous total.
bullets: Each page of your passbook shows a transaction and the running total.
The running total grows with every deposit added to it.
By the last page, the total reflects every transaction that happened.
analogy.highlightCard: An accumulator variable collects values across loop iterations — growing with each pass.

visualization.title: Accumulator Pattern
bullets: Start with a total variable set to 0 before the loop begins.
On each iteration, add the current item's value to the total.
After the loop, the total holds the combined result of all iterations.
visualization.highlightCard: total = 0 before the loop, total += value inside — the accumulator pattern.

code.code:
scores = [10, 20, 30]
total = 0
for s in scores:
    total += s
print("Sum:", total)
highlights: total = 0 initializes the accumulator before any loop runs.
total += score adds each score to the running total on every iteration.
After the loop, total holds the sum of all values in the list.
code.highlightCard: The accumulator pattern is the foundation of summing, counting, and collecting in Python.

reflection.question: Why do we initialize total = 0 BEFORE the loop?
reflection.answer: So we have a starting point to accumulate into. If we put it inside the loop, it would reset to 0 on every iteration.
options: So we have a starting point to add to
To avoid errors with empty lists
It doesn't matter where we put it

blocks.takeaway: A passbook accumulates transaction totals — just like an accumulator variable collects values across loop iterations. Initialize before the loop, add inside it, read after.

blocks.title: Grade Calculator
blocks.instructions: A teacher has 5 students' marks: [92, 78, 85, 63, 95]. Use a for loop to: 1) Calculate and print the total. 2) Calculate and print the class average. 3) Count and print how many students scored above 80.
blocks.starterCode:
marks = [92, 78, 85, 63, 95]
total = 0
above_80 = 0

# Loop through marks


# Print results
print(f"Total: {total}")
print(f"Average: {total / len(marks)}")
print(f"Above 80: {above_80}")
blocks.solution:
marks = [92, 78, 85, 63, 95]
total = 0
above_80 = 0

for mark in marks:
    total = total + mark
    if mark > 80:
        above_80 = above_80 + 1

print(f"Total: {total}")
print(f"Average: {total / len(marks)}")
print(f"Above 80: {above_80}")
blocks.hint: Inside the loop, add each mark to total. Use an if statement to check if mark > 80 and increment above_80.

keyTakeaways.text: A for loop repeats a block of code for each item in a sequence.
The loop variable holds the current item on each iteration.
range(stop), range(start, stop), range(start, stop, step) generate number sequences.
The accumulator pattern: initialize before the loop, update inside the loop.
enumerate() gives you both the index and the value in a single loop.
len() returns the number of items in a list — useful for averages.

whatYouLearned: How for loops work and how to write one
How to use range() with start, stop, and step
The accumulator pattern for computing totals and averages
How to use enumerate() for numbered iteration

quiz.question:
How many times will this loop run?
for i in range(3):
quiz.explanation: range(3) generates 0, 1, 2 — three numbers. The loop runs once for each value, so it runs 3 times.

quiz.question: What does range(2, 8, 2) generate?
quiz.explanation: range(2, 8, 2) starts at 2, goes up in steps of 2, and stops before 8. So: 2, 4, 6. It does NOT include 8.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the variable total = 0 before a loop that sums numbers?
options: It tells Python the loop type
It provides a starting point to accumulate the sum
It limits the number of iterations
quiz.answer: It provides a starting point to accumulate the sum
quiz.explanation: The accumulator variable must be initialised before the loop. If it were inside the loop, it would reset to 0 every iteration, making the final sum always equal the last element.

quiz.question: What will enumerate(['a', 'b', 'c'], start=1) produce?
quiz.explanation: enumerate() produces (index, value) pairs. start=1 makes the index begin at 1 instead of the default 0.

quiz.question:
What is the output of:
total = 0
for n in [2, 4, 6]:
    total += n
print(total)
quiz.explanation: total starts at 0. After each iteration: 0+2=2, 2+4=6, 6+6=12. The final total is 12. The += operator is shorthand for total = total + n.
